 C('Three similar forms, three meanings.','I USED TO read alone. → a former habit\nI AM USED TO reading aloud. → it is familiar\nI AM GETTING USED TO reading to a group. → adaptation is happening','Look for be or get before used to. Their presence changes both the meaning and the following verb form.'),
 C('Describe a former habit or state.','We used to meet after school.\nShe used to be shy.\n\nUsed to + base verb describes a past habit or state, usually contrasted with now.','For an ordinary current habit use present simple: We usually meet on Fridays.'),
 C('Use the base spelling after did.','Did you USE TO read aloud?\nI didn’t USE TO enjoy it.\n\nIn the standard written pattern, did/didn’t carries the past form and use stays in its base spelling.','Formal used not to is possible, but didn’t use to is the everyday pattern practised here.'),
 C('Be used to means accustomed to.','I’m used to the noise.\nShe was used to working with children.\n\nBe changes with the time. Used to is followed by a noun, pronoun or -ing activity.','Here to is a preposition. It does not introduce the base infinitive as it does in the former-habit pattern.'),
 C('Get used to describes adaptation.','I’m getting used to the new group.\nHe got used to answering questions.\nYou’ll get used to it.\n\nGet changes with the time; the following noun/-ing pattern stays the same.','Getting used to something does not say it is already completely familiar.'),
 C('Choose the right question.','Did you use to read here? → former habit\nAre you used to reading here? → familiar now\nAre you getting used to reading here? → adapting now','Do not use did for every expression containing used to. The actual verb pattern decides the helper.'),
 C('Separate state from change.','I wasn’t used to the noise at first.\nI gradually got used to it.\nNow I’m used to it.\n\nThese sentences describe initial unfamiliarity, adaptation and the resulting familiar state.','Be used to normally describes a state; get used to is useful when the process of change matters.'),
 C('Compare an old routine with a new one.','I used to plan every minute.\nNow I’m getting used to leaving space for questions.\n\nA short comparison can explain both what changed and how the new situation feels.','Hannah learns to work with lively reading sessions. Listen to the change in her approach, then describe an adaptation of your own.')
];

 G('edit','Correct: She is used to speak in front of a group.','She is used to speaking in front of a group.','After is used to, to is a preposition and the activity takes -ing.','The word is before used to changes the pattern. It describes familiarity rather than a former speaking habit.'),

 G('rewrite','Use be used to for present familiarity: Early starts are normal for me.  G('rewrite','Use get used to in past simple: Gradually, the noise became familiar to me.  G('choice','Choose the correct sentence for a current ordinary habit.','I usually read with the group on Wednesdays.','Present simple with usually describes a current habit.  G('edit','Correct the question about adaptation: Do you getting used to the timetable?','Are you getting used to the timetable?','Present continuous getting needs the helper are before you in the question.','The -ing form describes an adaptation in progress.  G('order','Build a negative sentence about former behaviour.','We didn’t use to plan every minute.','Didn’t use to + base verb describes the absence of a former habitual behaviour.','Keep the negative helper before use to. The main activity stays in its base form.'),

'use strict';
const {C,G,A,V}=require('./lesson-authoring.cjs');
const cards=[
 C('Describe a routine from another time.','When we were children, we used to stay by the sea.\nEvery morning, we would walk to the harbour.\n\nUsed to introduces former routines or states. Would can bring repeated past actions to life.','A clear past-time setting helps the listener interpret would as a habit rather than a conditional.'),
 C('Use used to for actions and states.','We used to travel by train. → action\nWe used to own a small car. → possession/state\nI used to be shy. → state\n\nThe expression usually contrasts the past with now.','Past simple also describes past habits and states. Used to makes the former pattern more explicit.'),
 C('Use would for repeated actions.','Every summer, we would visit our cousins.\nAfter breakfast, Dad would check the map.\n\nIn a past narrative, would + base verb can describe characteristic repeated events.','For simple continuous past states such as owning a house, use used to or past simple instead.'),
 C('Set the period before the routine.','When I lived by the coast, I would walk along the beach every evening.\n\nThe opening establishes the period. Every evening makes the repeated action clear.','Without context, I would walk may express an imagined choice rather than a memory.'),
 C('Do not turn one event into a habit.','Last Saturday, our train was cancelled. → one event\nOn summer trips, trains would sometimes be crowded. → repeated experience\n\nA single completed event normally needs past simple.','Used to and habitual would are not general replacements for every past-tense verb.'),
 C('Keep negative and question forms useful.','Did you use to go there?\nWe didn’t use to book ahead.\n\nUse the base spelling use after did/didn’t. These are clear everyday ways to ask about former routines.','Wouldn’t may describe repeated refusal, so it is not always a neutral replacement for didn’t use to.'),

'use strict';
const {C,G,A,V}=require('./lesson-authoring.cjs');
const cards=[
 C('Look at a future moment in two ways.','At six, we WILL BE SORTING the clothes. → activity in progress\nBy six, we WILL HAVE SORTED the clothes. → completion before that point\n\nThe focus is progress versus completion.','Choose the view the listener needs.  C('Build future continuous.','Will + be + -ing.\nI’ll be working at ten.\nWill you be using the room?\nWe won’t be staying late.','The first helper forms the question or negative. Keep be before the -ing verb.'),
 C('Describe activity around a time.','This time tomorrow, we’ll be setting up the event.\nWhen you arrive, I’ll be helping at the entrance.\n\nFuture continuous places an activity around a future reference point.','It can also present an expected plan or routine without stressing a new decision.'),
 C('Ask about plans politely.','Will you be using the table this afternoon?\n\nThis can sound like a neutral enquiry about an expected plan. Will you use it? may sound more like a request or a decision question.','Tone and context matter. The continuous form does not make every sentence automatically polite.'),
 C('Build future perfect.','Will + have + past participle.\nWe’ll have finished by Friday.\nWill they have checked it by noon?\nShe won’t have arrived by then.','Use the participle after have: written, gone, finished. Do not use a past-simple form such as wrote.'),
 C('Use a deadline or an endpoint.','By noon → no later than noon\nBy the time you arrive → before that future point\n\nBy next June, we’ll have known each other for a year.\nFuture perfect can also measure a state’s duration up to a future time.','A deadline can also occur with simple future: I’ll finish by Friday. Future perfect explicitly looks back from the endpoint.'),
 C('Keep future time clauses in the present.','When she arrives, we’ll be sorting the clothes.\nBy the time you get here, we’ll have finished.\n\nIn these future time clauses, use a present form rather than will.','This rule concerns time clauses.  C('Make a useful project update.','At two, I’ll be checking the donations.\nBy four, we’ll have labelled everything.\n\nGive both the activity at a moment and a result expected before a deadline.','Sofia discusses the hidden costs of clothing. Listen to her reasoning, then plan a small repair, reuse or clothes-exchange project.')
];

 G('gap','At ten tomorrow, I will be ___ the donated clothes. Use the -ing form of sort.','sorting','Future continuous needs will + be + an -ing verb, here sorting.','The helper sequence already presents an activity in progress. Add the activity form after be.'),
 G('choice','Choose a correctly formed future continuous sentence.','We’ll be preparing the room at noon.','Future continuous uses will be followed by the -ing main verb.','Check the verb parts after will.  G('choice','Which form is normally used for the state know up to a future endpoint?','By June, we’ll have known each other for a year.','Know is normally stative, so the simple perfect form describes its duration up to June.','The sentence describes knowing someone rather than an action being performed.  G('gap','Will they ___ finished by three? Add the missing perfect helper.','have','The question keeps will before the subject and have + finished after it.','The intended form is future perfect. The subject does not change have to has after a modal.'),

 G('edit','Correct: She will be work at that time.','She will be working at that time.','Future continuous needs an -ing main verb after will be.','The sentence describes what will be in progress at a future time. Change the main verb form only.'),

 G('rewrite','Make a future perfect negative: They will have completed the repairs by noon.','They will not have completed the repairs by noon.|They won’t have completed the repairs by noon.','Not attaches to will, while have completed remains the perfect part of the structure.','Change the first helper to a negative.  A('choice','What had made unnecessary buying too easy for her?','The low price.','She connects the low cost of individual purchases with buying things she did not need.','the low price had made it too easy to buy things I did not really need.','Identify the cause she names when looking at the pile of clothes, rather than an invented advertising offer.',['The low price.','A rule requiring a different outfit every day.','Having no shops near her home.']),

 A('choice','Which qualification does Sofia make about quality?','Cheap clothes are not always badly made.','Her argument is qualified rather than a claim that every inexpensive item has the same quality.','Cheap clothes are not always badly made','Notice not always.  A('choice','Why does she not simply tell everyone to buy expensive ethical brands?','She recognises that this is unrealistic for many people.','She acknowledges different financial circumstances and proposes smaller changes as alternatives.','That is not realistic for many people.','Her practical suggestions follow a limitation about what people can reasonably afford or access.',['She recognises that this is unrealistic for many people.','She says price is the only important issue.','She believes repairing clothes is impossible.']),
 A('sequence','Put these parts of Sofia’s account in order.',['She enjoys buying inexpensive clothes.','She discovers unused items in her wardrobe.','She learns about wider production and waste costs.','She changes her questions before buying.'],'Her personal experience leads to research, then practical changes in buying behaviour.','Now, before I buy something, I ask myself three questions','Follow the movement from her former habit to the personal discovery and then the new approach.'),

'use strict';
const {C,G,A,V}=require('./lesson-authoring.cjs');
const cards=[
 C('Separate a routine from one possibility.','If I work late, I feel tired. → a general personal pattern\nIf I work late tonight, I’ll call you. → a specific future possibility\n\nZero conditional commonly uses present forms in both clauses.  C('Build a real future condition.','If you help, we’ll finish sooner.\nIf it rains, we can stay inside.\nIf you see a problem, tell me.\n\nThe result may use will, another suitable modal or an imperative.','Use a present form in the ordinary if-clause, not a future will form.'),
 C('Use different present forms when needed.','If she’s working, don’t interrupt.\nIf you’ve finished, we can begin.\n\nPresent continuous can show activity in progress; present perfect can highlight completion of the condition.','The rule is not limited to present simple.  C('Choose if or when deliberately.','If Leo joins, we’ll start at six. → joining is uncertain\nWhen Leo arrives, we’ll start. → arrival is treated as expected\n\nFor general routines, when and if can often both fit.','Do not turn uncertainty into a certainty just by changing the linker.'),
 C('Unless means except if.','We won’t start unless everyone is ready.\n→ We won’t start if everyone is not ready.\n\nUnless already provides the except-if condition.  C('State a requirement or take a precaution.','You can join as long as you register. → condition\nI’ll bring an umbrella in case it rains. → precaution\n\nIn case is not simply another word for if: the umbrella is brought before knowing whether rain will happen.','Provided that can introduce a requirement too, often in a more formal style.'),
 C('Use future time clauses alongside conditions.','When the class ends, we’ll tidy up.\nWe won’t leave until everyone has finished.\n\nThese present forms describe future timing. If you need help, ask. describes a condition.','A time clause and a condition can look similar but organise different relationships.'),
 C('Keep the plan clear and realistic.','If we have enough helpers, we’ll run another session.\nBefore you leave, confirm the time.\n\nA comma normally follows an opening if/time clause.\n\nPolite willingness is a special use: If you’ll wait here…','Marcus tells how Leo changed his work gradually. ];

 G('rewrite','Use unless without changing the intended condition: We won’t start if everyone is not ready.','We won’t start unless everyone is ready.|We will not start unless everyone is ready.','Unless everyone is ready expresses the except-if condition while keeping the negative result.','Keep won’t start and make readiness the positive condition following unless.'),

 G('edit','Correct the ordinary future condition: If we will have enough helpers, we’ll run a session.','If we have enough helpers, we’ll run a session.|If we have enough helpers, we will run a session.','The ordinary if-clause uses present have; will remains in the predicted result.','This is a resource condition, not a special use of will for willingness.  G('rewrite','Put the condition first: We can begin if everyone has arrived.','If everyone has arrived, we can begin.','The present-perfect condition may come first and normally takes a comma before the main modal result.','Move the whole if-clause.  G('choice','In “If you’ll wait here, I’ll get the organiser”, will in the if-clause can express…','polite willingness to wait.','This is a special willingness use, unlike the ordinary future condition that normally takes a present form.','Do not apply a rule that will is impossible after every if.  C('Give hypothetical advice.','If I were you, I would ask the guide.\n\nWere is the usual careful form in this advice expression.  C('Imagine a different past.','If we had booked earlier, we would have joined the tour.\n\nThird conditional: if + had + past participle → would/could/might + have + past participle.  C('Use the right past form.','If she hadn’t been rushing, she might have noticed the sign.\nIf he had checked, he could have avoided the mistake.\n\nPast perfect continuous can highlight an earlier activity. 'use strict';
const {C,G,A,V}=require('./lesson-authoring.cjs');
const cards=[
 C('Wish for a different situation now.','I wish the instructions were clearer.\nIf only I had more time!\n\nWish / if only + past form describes a situation you want to be different now. The form marks distance from reality.','The past form here does not mean the wish concerns yesterday. Decide which time the desired change belongs to.'),
 C('Include ability and ongoing situations.','I wish I could explain it better. → ability\nI wish we were working together. → ongoing situation\n\nWas occurs in everyday usage; were is a common careful choice after I/he/she/it in unreal wishes.','Use could for ability. Do not add would automatically to every sentence after I wish.'),
 C('Regret a finished past action.','I wish I had checked the report.\nIf only I hadn’t sent that email!\n\nWish + past perfect imagines a different past. Had + past participle keeps the regret in the finished past.','A present wish about a past event needs an earlier-past form: I wish I had asked, rather than I wish I ask.'),
 C('Regret an opportunity you could not take.','I wish I could have attended the meeting.\n\nCould have + past participle can express regret about an unavailable past opportunity or ability.\nI wish I hadn’t been rushing. highlights an ongoing past activity.','Choose the form that matches the regret: a past action, a missed possibility or an ongoing past activity.'),
 C('Ask for a change with would.','I wish you would let me finish.\nI wish it would stop raining.\n\nWould expresses a desired change, often with annoyance, about behaviour or a situation outside the speaker’s control.','This can sound like a complaint. In feedback, a calm direct request may suit the relationship better.'),
 C('Use if only for stronger feeling.','If only the room were quieter!\nIf only I had listened!\nIf only they would reply!\n\nThe same time patterns work, but if only often adds stronger emotion.','An exclamation mark can show the tone. The grammar still depends on whether the wish concerns now, the past or a desired change.'),
 C('Choose hope for a realistic possibility.','I hope she replies tomorrow. → a realistic future possibility\nI wish she were here. → she is not here now\nI wish she would reply. → a desired change, often frustration','Hope and wish are not interchangeable tense frames. Say what you believe is possible and choose the tone deliberately.'),
 C('Turn a wish into useful feedback.','I wish the report were clearer. states a desired difference.\nPlease label the three missing figures. gives an actionable request.\n\nA wish can explain your feeling, but a specific next step makes feedback useful.','Julia discusses honesty, respect and timing. Listen to her reasoning, then use wishes without turning them into personal criticism.')
];
const tasks=[
 G('choice','Which sentence expresses a wish about the present?','I wish the room were quieter.','The past form were marks a desired difference in the present rather than a completed past regret.','Look for a situation that is different from what the speaker wants now, without had plus a participle.',['I wish the room were quieter.','I wish I had checked yesterday.','I hope the room is free tomorrow.']),
 G('gap','I wish I ___ explain this more clearly. Use could or had.','could','Could followed by a base verb expresses a wish for a different ability in the present.','The following verb is explain, with no participle. Choose the form that expresses present ability.'),
 G('order','Build a wish about a current situation.','I wish we had more time to talk.','Had here is the past form of have, marking an unreal present situation after wish.','The speaker wants more time now. Keep I wish first, followed by the subject of the desired situation.'),
 G('edit','Correct the past regret: I wish I have checked the figures yesterday.','I wish I had checked the figures yesterday.','Yesterday places the regretted action in the finished past, requiring past perfect after wish.','Identify the regretted action’s time. Replace the present-perfect helper with the earlier-past helper.'),
 G('choice','Which form expresses a finished-past regret?','I wish I had asked earlier.','Had asked is past perfect, the usual pattern for imagining a different action in the finished past.','Look for had plus a participle, rather than a present ability wish or a realistic future hope.',['I wish I had asked earlier.','I wish I could ask now.','I hope I can ask tomorrow.']),
 G('gap','If only I hadn’t ___ that email. Use send.','sent','Hadn’t needs the past participle sent to express regret about the earlier completed action.','The auxiliary is already provided. Choose the irregular participle of send rather than adding another helper.'),
 G('choice','“I wish you would stop interrupting” often conveys…','a desired behaviour change with annoyance.','Would stop presents the change the speaker wants from someone else, often with a complaining tone.','Consider the interpersonal tone and the repeated behaviour.  G('order','Build a regret about a missed past opportunity.','I wish I could have attended the meeting.','Could have attended expresses regret about an opportunity or ability that was unavailable in the past.','Keep could with have and the participle. The meeting belongs to the past, rather than a current ability.'),
 G('edit','Correct the present wish using a past form: I wish the task is easier.','I wish the task were easier.|I wish the task was easier.','Were or everyday was marks the desired difference from the current situation after I wish.','The task is difficult now. Use the unreal-past pattern after wish; careful were and everyday was are accepted.'),
 G('gap','I wish they ___ reply to my messages. Use would to express a desired change.','would','Would reply describes a change in another person’s behaviour that the speaker wants to happen.','The prompt asks for a desired change in behaviour, not a completed regret.  G('choice','Which sentence presents a realistic future hope?','I hope she passes tomorrow.','Hope with a present form can refer to a realistic future event, unlike an unreal-present wish.','Look for the hopeful possibility rather than the pattern used to describe a situation contrary to fact.',['I hope she passes tomorrow.','I wish she passed yesterday.','I wish she will passes tomorrow.']),
 G('rewrite','Start with If only: I wish I had listened.','If only I had listened.|If only I had listened!','If only keeps the past-perfect regret and typically gives the statement a stronger emotional tone.','Replace the opening frame while preserving had listened. The regret still concerns a completed past event.'),
 G('order','Build a wish about an ongoing situation.','I wish we were working together today.','Past continuous after wish describes a desired ongoing situation contrary to the present arrangement.','Today anchors the wish in the present. Keep were with the activity form working after the subject.'),
 G('gap','I wish I hadn’t been ___ during the discussion. Use rush.','rushing','Hadn’t been rushing expresses regret about an activity that was ongoing in the past discussion.','The earlier-past continuous helpers are supplied. Complete them with the appropriate activity form.'),
 G('choice','Which phrase correctly describes a past regret about ability?','I wish I could have helped.','Could have helped describes a past ability or opportunity the speaker wishes had been available.','Look for a modal-perfect form that keeps the missed ability in the past rather than projecting it into tomorrow.',['I wish I could have helped.','I wish I can have help.','I wish I would helped.']),
 G('edit','Use the usual ability pattern: I wish I would speak French fluently.','I wish I could speak French fluently.','Could is the usual choice for a wish about the speaker’s own ability, rather than a complaint with would.','The issue is personal language ability, not someone else’s willingness to change behaviour. Choose the ability modal.'),
 G('rewrite','Express a past regret with wish: I didn’t read the comments, and I regret that now.','I wish I had read the comments.','The speaker regrets not doing a completed past action, so wish is followed by positive past perfect.','The real action was negative: the comments were not read.  G('choice','Which follow-up makes feedback more actionable?','Please label the three missing figures.','A specific request names the observable change needed, which is more useful than an unclear personal complaint.','Choose a concrete change the recipient can make, rather than a judgement about their whole personality.',['Please label the three missing figures.','I wish you were a better person.','Just make everything much better somehow.'])
];
const listening=[
 A('choice','What balance does Julia say good feedback needs?','Honesty and respect.','She explains that excessive bluntness can hurt while excessive softness can make feedback unhelpful.','Good feedback needs two things that are hard to balance: honesty and respect.','Listen for the pair that makes feedback both clear and considerate, rather than assuming kindness alone is enough.',['Honesty and respect.','Speed and complete agreement.','Praise and silence about every problem.']),
 A('choice','Why can a comment about a report feel personal?','People may hear it as a judgement about their ability.','The listener may translate criticism of one report into criticism of their whole professional identity.','it can feel personal.','Connect the example of an unclear report to the explanation about identity, rather than taking the words only literally.',['People may hear it as a judgement about their ability.','Every report comment is a legal accusation.','Managers always intend to insult employees.']),
 A('choice','What is the problem with very vague gentle feedback?','The recipient may not understand what to change.','Soft language can avoid a clear message, leaving the employee without an actionable understanding.','without understanding what needs to change.','Focus on what the employee can do after the conversation, rather than whether the manager sounds friendly.',['The recipient may not understand what to change.','It always gives an exact correction automatically.','It guarantees that the employee agrees.']),
 A('gap','How many missing numbers appear in Julia’s specific report example?','3|three','Julia replaces a personality judgement with an example of three missing numbers and a practical check.','There were three missing numbers in the last report','The number belongs to the concrete example of useful feedback, not to the number of feedback methods.'),
 A('choice','Why can feedback given much too late feel unfair?','The person may no longer remember the situation clearly.','A delayed discussion can be hard to connect to the event and therefore feel less fair or helpful.','the person no longer remembers the situation clearly.','Listen to the separate reasons for feedback during stress and feedback after a long delay.',['The person may no longer remember the situation clearly.','Old feedback is always more accurate than recent feedback.','The speaker says timing never changes the effect.']),
 A('choice','What does Julia advise when receiving feedback?','Listen, ask questions and separate the message from the feeling.','The advice supports understanding the feedback before reacting, without requiring acceptance of every comment.','It helps to listen first, ask questions, and separate the message from the uncomfortable feeling.','Choose the response that supports understanding while leaving room to question whether a comment is fair.',['Listen, ask questions and separate the message from the feeling.','Accept every comment as unquestionably correct.','Defend yourself before hearing the whole message.']),
 A('sequence','Order these ideas as Julia presents them.',['Feedback can feel connected to identity.','Gentle language can become too vague.','Useful feedback focuses on behaviour.','Receiving feedback requires listening and questions.'],'The explanation moves from emotional difficulty to giving useful feedback and then to receiving it.','Receiving feedback is also a skill.','Follow the argument’s development rather than arranging the statements into your own preferred advice sequence.'),
 A('choice','Does Julia say every piece of feedback is correct?','No; some comments are unfair or based on limited information.','She encourages learning and questions while acknowledging that feedback itself can be mistaken or unfair.','Sometimes feedback is unfair or based on limited information.','Pay attention to the qualification after the receiving-feedback advice, rather than assuming unconditional acceptance.',['No; some comments are unfair or based on limited information.','Yes; the listener must accept every comment.','No feedback can ever contain anything useful.'])
];
const vocab=[V('defensive','quick to protect yourself against criticism','Julia describes this reaction before someone has fully listened. It concerns emotional self-protection rather than a physical shield.'),V('vague','not clear or specific enough','A gentle message can sound this way if it does not show what must change. Think of unclear meaning, not a quiet voice.'),V('behaviour','the way someone acts','Julia recommends focusing feedback here instead of judging personality. It refers to observable actions in a situation.'),V('respect','consideration for someone’s feelings and dignity','Julia pairs this with honesty. Think of a final time for completing a task, not when it begins.'),V('unfair','not reasonable or just in the circumstances','Julia admits that some comments are like this. The word evaluates fairness rather than whether feedback feels uncomfortable.')];

'use strict';
const {C,G,A,V}=require('./lesson-authoring.cjs');
const cards=[
 C('Infer what happened from evidence.','The shop is dark, and the door is locked. They must have closed early.\n\nModal + have + past participle lets you make a deduction about the past. It does not turn an inference into direct knowledge.','Look for evidence and choose a suitable degree of certainty. Avoid assigning fixed numerical percentages to these modals.'),
 C('Use must have for a strong conclusion.','She knew every detail. She must have read the report.\n\nMust have + participle expresses a strong positive deduction about the past, not an obligation to act in the past.','For past obligation, use had to. Must have read describes what the speaker concludes, not what someone was required to do.'),
 C('Use can’t or couldn’t for a strong negative deduction.','Her flight landed at nine. She can’t have arrived here at eight.\nThat couldn’t have been Leo: he was abroad.\n\nCan’t/couldn’t have + participle presents a past explanation as impossible.','Mustn’t usually expresses prohibition, not the normal strong negative deduction taught here. Its use can vary across dialects and contexts.'),
 C('Leave possibilities open.','The parcel may have gone to the wrong address.\nThey might have missed the message.\nThe customer could have misunderstood.\n\nThese suggest possible explanations without claiming certainty.','Could have can also describe an unused opportunity: You could have called, but you didn’t. Context distinguishes the meanings.'),
 C('Make a possibility negative.','They might not have heard us.\nShe may not have seen the sign.\n\nThese keep non-occurrence possible. Compare: She can’t have seen it. presents seeing it as impossible.','Do not automatically replace might not have with couldn’t have. That can change a weak possibility into a strong negative conclusion.'),
 C('Distinguish expectation from criticism.','The parcel should have arrived by now. → expected result; check the context\nYou should have checked the address. → criticism of an omission\nYou shouldn’t have shared the code. → criticism of an action','Ought to have can express similar meanings. Should is followed by have; ought keeps to before have.'),
 C('Add ongoing or passive meaning.','They must have been working late. → earlier activity\nThe file might have been deleted. → passive\n\nQuestions invert the modal: Could they have left early?\nAfter have, use gone / seen / written, not went / saw / wrote.','Keep the first modal, then have, then the forms needed for the intended meaning. Do not add to after must, might or should.'),
 C('Separate evidence from judgement.','The family shop faced rising costs. That is reported in Grace’s story.\nThey must have felt worried. That is a deduction.\nThey should have changed sooner. That is a judgement.','Listen for the reported facts first. Then make cautious inferences and explain what supports them, without inventing proof.')
];
const tasks=[
 G('choice','Which phrase expresses a strong positive deduction about the past?','She must have read it.','Must have read presents the earlier reading as a strong conclusion drawn from evidence.','Look for deduction about a past action rather than present obligation or a weak possibility.',['She must have read it.','She must read it tomorrow.','She might read it next week.']),
 G('gap','He must have ___ the email. Use see.','seen','Have is followed by the participle seen, giving the required modal-perfect form for a past deduction.','The modal and have are already supplied. Complete the structure with the irregular participle, not the past-simple form.'),
 G('order','Build a strong negative past deduction.','She can’t have arrived before eight.','Can’t have arrived presents the earlier arrival as impossible according to the speaker’s evidence.','Keep the modal before have and the participle. Place the time phrase after the completed verb group.'),
 G('edit','Correct the participle: They might have went to the other shop.','They might have gone to the other shop.','Might have requires the participle gone rather than the past-simple went in a past possibility.','The degree of certainty is already suitable. Correct only the verb form following have.'),
 G('choice','Which sentence leaves open the possibility that no one heard?','They might not have heard us.','Might not have heard describes possible non-occurrence, without claiming that hearing was impossible.','Choose a weak negative possibility, rather than a strong exclusion or a statement of certainty.',['They might not have heard us.','They can’t have heard us.','They definitely heard us.']),
 G('gap','The file might have ___ deleted. Complete the passive.','been','Modal-perfect passive uses might have been plus a past participle to focus on what happened to the file.','Deleted describes the action received by the file. Complete the passive group between have and that participle.'),
 G('choice','“You could have called, but you didn’t” describes…','an opportunity that was not used.','The final clause confirms the call did not happen, making could have an unused opportunity here.','Use the full sentence, especially but you didn’t.  G('order','Build a possible explanation about an ongoing past activity.','They might have been working late.','Might have been working describes a possible earlier activity in progress rather than a completed quantity.','Keep might have been together before the activity form. The final word describes when the work occurred.'),
 G('edit','Use the ordinary negative deduction: He mustn’t have been there; he was abroad.','He can’t have been there; he was abroad.|He couldn’t have been there; he was abroad.','Can’t or couldn’t have been is the ordinary strong negative deduction supported by the evidence of being abroad.','The evidence rules out his presence.  G('gap','You should ___ checked the figures first.  G('choice','In “The parcel should have arrived by now”, should can express…','an expected result by the present time.','Should have arrived can describe an expectation, and does not by itself prove that the parcel failed to arrive.','Do not assume every should have sentence is criticism. Look at the delivery expectation and the phrase by now.',['an expected result by the present time.','a certainty that the parcel is lost forever.','an order to post it next year.']),
 G('rewrite','Make a past-deduction question: They could have left early.','Could they have left early?','A question puts the modal could before the subject and keeps have left together afterwards.','Move only the first modal before they. Keep the past-perfect infinitive and end with question punctuation.'),
 G('order','Build a strong conclusion from past evidence.','She must have known about the change.','Must have known expresses a strong inference about an earlier state of knowledge.','Use the modal-perfect group for the deduction. About the change describes what she is inferred to have known.'),
 G('gap','He ought ___ have warned us. Complete the pattern.','to','Ought keeps to before have, unlike should have, while both can evaluate an earlier action.','This modal-like expression differs from should. Complete its fixed form before the perfect infinitive.'),
 G('choice','Which contrast correctly distinguishes obligation and deduction?','Had to leave = obligation; must have left = deduction.','Had to describes an earlier requirement, whereas must have left is a conclusion about what happened.','Decide whether the sentence requires an action or infers that an action occurred; these are different meanings.',['Had to leave = obligation; must have left = deduction.','Must have left always means a rule forced them to leave.','Had to leave always means the speaker is guessing.']),
 G('edit','Correct the modal pattern: She may to have missed the call.','She may have missed the call.','May takes the bare perfect infinitive have missed, so no to is used after the modal.','The past possibility is suitable. Remove the extra infinitive marker between may and have.'),
 G('rewrite','Express a cautious past possibility using might: Perhaps the customer misunderstood.','The customer might have misunderstood.','Might have misunderstood expresses an uncertain explanation of a completed past event.','Keep the customer as subject.  G('choice','Which sentence marks an inference rather than a reported fact?','They must have felt worried about the costs.','Must have felt explicitly presents a conclusion about their feelings rather than a directly reported event.','Look for a modal showing the speaker’s reasoning. ];

 A('choice','How is the shop described today?','Smaller than before, but still operating.','Survival did not mean returning to its former size; the business found a viable new direction.','the shop is smaller than it used to be, but it is alive.','Use the final description. 'use strict';
const {C,G,A,V}=require('./lesson-authoring.cjs');
const cards=[
 C('Predict without pretending to know.','The app is likely to help. → probable\nIt might interrupt us. → possible\nIt is unlikely to save time. → improbable\n\nThese expressions show the speaker’s judgement, not a measured guarantee.','Use the context and evidence to choose a level of confidence. These words do not correspond to fixed numerical probabilities.'),
 C('Build likely and unlikely patterns.','The team is likely to finish.\nIt is unlikely that they will agree.\n\nPerson/thing + be + likely/unlikely + to + base verb\nIt + be + likely/unlikely + that + clause','Likely can also be used as an adverb, especially in American English. For this lesson, practise the useful be likely to and it is likely that patterns.'),
 C('Express a strong prediction.','There is bound to be a delay.\nShe is sure to notice.\nThe meeting is certain to be busy.\n\nBe bound/sure/certain to expresses strong confidence about an outcome.','Bound to is not the same as a legal obligation. A confident prediction can still be wrong.'),
 C('Place probably and definitely clearly.','They will probably reply.\nShe is definitely available.\nHe probably won’t join.\nThey will probably not finish.\n\nThese adverbs usually go before the main verb, after be or an affirmative auxiliary.','In ordinary negative predictions, probably/definitely often go before won’t. Full will not also allows will probably not.'),
 C('Use maybe and perhaps for a whole idea.','Maybe we should wait.\nPerhaps the update will help.\n\nMaybe and perhaps often come at the beginning of a clause. Maybe is one word; may be is a modal plus the verb be.','Maybe it is useful and It may be useful can express similar possibilities, but their grammar differs.'),
 C('Use possibility modals with care.','We may need more time.\nThe tool might distract us.\nThis could work.\nIt might not help.\n\nMay, might and could express possibilities. Their strength depends on context, not a universal ranking.','Might not keeps non-occurrence possible. Can’t usually rules something out, so it does not have the same meaning.'),
 C('Describe a chance.','There is a good chance that they will accept.\nThere is little chance of success.\nThey are more likely to agree now.\n\nChance can be followed by a that-clause or of + noun/-ing. Likely allows modifiers such as quite, very and more.','A statement about likelihood is different from a statement of fact. Explain why you expect an outcome when the situation calls for it.'),
 C('Test a promise against experience.','The app promised to improve Nathan’s work. His experience was different.\n\nA simpler system is likely to be easier to maintain. This is a prediction you can test.','Listen for actual effects, not just promised benefits. Then recommend a realistic tool or routine without promising guaranteed productivity.')
];
const tasks=[
 G('choice','Which sentence uses the be likely to pattern?','The team is likely to finish today.','Be likely to is followed by a base verb and presents finishing as probable rather than certain.','Look for the adjective after be and a to-infinitive afterwards. 'use strict';
const {C,G,A,V}=require('./lesson-authoring.cjs');
const cards=[
 C('Say what is necessary.','I need to confirm the time.\nWe will need to bring tickets.\n\nNeed as a main verb takes to + base verb. Questions and negatives use do/does/did: Do you need to leave?','Necessity depends on the situation. Do not confuse something useful with something that is required.'),
 C('Remove a requirement without banning an action.','You don’t need to bring food.\nYou needn’t bring food.\n\nBoth say it is not necessary. Needn’t is a modal-like form, especially in British English: no to and no third-person -s.','You may still bring food if you want. Mustn’t bring food means bringing it is forbidden, a different meaning.'),
 C('Describe past lack of necessity.','We didn’t need to queue, so we went straight in.\n\nDidn’t need to means there was no necessity. Context may tell us whether the action happened; the phrase alone does not always settle that.','We didn’t need to book, but we booked anyway is possible. Avoid treating didn’t need to as proof an action never happened.'),
 C('Say an action happened unnecessarily.','We needn’t have queued: the entrance was free.\n\nNeedn’t have + past participle normally makes clear that the action did happen but was unnecessary.','Compare the fact of doing the action with the absence of a requirement. This contrast is more precise than only comparing past verb forms.'),
 C('Ask and answer naturally.','Do we need to register?\nYes, we do. / No, we don’t.\n\nFormal British English also has Need I say more?\nYou won’t need to print anything. removes a future requirement.','Main-verb need uses ordinary do-support. Modal needn’t does not need another do auxiliary.'),
 C('Use no need and passive meaning.','There is no need to hurry.\nThere is no need for an apology.\nThe windows need cleaning.\n= The windows need to be cleaned.','Need + -ing can have passive meaning, especially in British English. The windows do not perform the cleaning themselves.'),
 C('Tell necessity from prohibition.','You needn’t share personal information. → not required\nYou mustn’t share the access code. → prohibited\nAll you need to do is click Confirm. → one required action','Choose the intended meaning before the form. A friendly invitation should not accidentally become a rule or a ban.'),
 C('Keep a small conversation manageable.','You don’t need to give a long speech.\nYou can ask one friendly question and listen.\n\nNora’s experiment involves short exchanges, not an obligation to make every encounter deep.','Listen for her actual rule and its limits. Practise explaining requirements and choices without forcing a conversation.')
];
const tasks=[
 G('choice','Which sentence says something is optional rather than forbidden?','You don’t need to bring a notebook.','Don’t need to removes a requirement without banning the action, unlike mustn’t.','Decide whether the action is allowed but unnecessary, or not allowed at all. The question asks for optional.',['You don’t need to bring a notebook.','You mustn’t bring a notebook.','You are forbidden to bring a notebook.']),
 G('gap','Do we need ___ book a table? Complete the main-verb pattern.','to','Need as a main verb takes a to-infinitive, even when the question uses the auxiliary do.','Do already forms the question. Complete the infinitive structure between need and the base verb book.'),
 G('order','Build a modal-like statement of no necessity.','You needn’t bring anything tomorrow.','Needn’t takes a bare infinitive and means that bringing something is not required tomorrow.','Do not add to after the modal-like form. Keep the base verb directly after needn’t.'),
 G('edit','Correct the modal-like pattern: She needn’t to wait.','She needn’t wait.','Needn’t is followed by a bare infinitive, so to is removed and no third-person -s is added.','This sentence uses modal-like needn’t rather than main-verb need. Remove the unnecessary infinitive marker.'),
 G('choice','What does “We didn’t need to book” establish by itself?','There was no necessity; context tells us whether we booked.','Didn’t need to states lack of necessity, but can be followed by but we booked anyway.','Do not assume the action’s occurrence from this phrase alone. Separate necessity from what actually happened.',['There was no necessity; context tells us whether we booked.','It always proves that no booking happened.','It proves booking was forbidden.']),
 G('gap','We needn’t have ___ the tickets. Use print.','printed','Needn’t have printed says the printing occurred but was unnecessary, using a past participle after have.','The perfect auxiliary is already present. Add the participle for the completed but unnecessary action.'),
 G('choice','Which sentence makes clear that the action happened unnecessarily?','We needn’t have waited.','Needn’t have waited normally presents the waiting as an action that occurred without being necessary.','Look for the perfect form that explicitly evaluates a completed action as unnecessary.',['We needn’t have waited.','We won’t need to wait.','Do we need to wait?']),
 G('order','Build a question using need as a main verb.','Do you need to leave now?','Main-verb need uses do before the subject and a to-infinitive before the action.','Begin with the question auxiliary and the subject. Keep need to leave as the main-verb group.'),
 G('edit','Correct the main-verb negative: He doesn’t needs to register.','He doesn’t need to register.','After doesn’t, the main verb uses the base form need, so the third-person ending is removed.','Doesn’t already carries the present-simple agreement. Use the uninflected main verb after that auxiliary.'),
 G('gap','The windows need ___. Use clean in the -ing pattern with passive meaning.','cleaning','Need cleaning means need to be cleaned: the windows receive rather than perform the action.','The prompt asks for the short -ing construction. Think of work that someone must do to the windows.'),
 G('choice','Which sentence expresses prohibition?','You mustn’t share the code.','Mustn’t makes sharing prohibited, whereas needn’t and don’t need to only remove necessity.','Choose the form that says the action is not allowed, rather than merely saying it can be skipped.',['You mustn’t share the code.','You needn’t share the code.','You don’t need to share the code.']),
 G('rewrite','Use needn’t have: We printed the form, but printing it was unnecessary.','We needn’t have printed the form.','Needn’t have printed combines the completed action with the information that it was unnecessary.','Both facts matter: the printing occurred and it was not needed. Use the perfect form that preserves both.'),
 G('order','Build a future statement of no necessity.','You won’t need to bring lunch tomorrow.','Won’t need to removes the future requirement, with need followed by the to-infinitive.','Keep the future negative before need. Unlike needn’t, this main-verb pattern retains to before bring.'),
 G('gap','There is no need ___ an apology. Use for or to.','for','No need for takes a noun phrase; an apology is a noun phrase rather than an infinitive action.','Look at what follows the gap. Use the preposition for a noun, not the marker used before a base verb.'),
 G('choice','“The car needs washing” means…','Someone needs to wash the car.','The -ing pattern after need has passive meaning: the car receives the washing.','Identify who receives the action. The car does not perform the activity, despite the -ing form.',['Someone needs to wash the car.','The car wants to wash another vehicle.','Washing the car is forbidden.']),
 G('edit','Correct the main-verb question: Did you needed to wait?','Did you need to wait?','Did forms the past question, so the following main verb is the base form need.','The past time is already marked by did. Remove the extra past ending from the main verb.'),
 G('rewrite','Use no need to: You don’t need to hurry.','There is no need to hurry.|There’s no need to hurry.','There is no need to followed by a base verb expresses the same absence of a requirement to hurry.','Use the impersonal there is frame and keep an infinitive after need. Preserve the optional rather than forbidden meaning.'),
 G('choice','Choose the reply to “Do I need to give a long speech?” that removes pressure.','No, you don’t. A friendly question is enough.','The short answer matches do and clarifies that a long speech is not required in this situation.','Choose an answer that removes the requirement and offers a manageable alternative without forbidding speech.',['No, you don’t. A friendly question is enough.','No, you mustn’t ever speak to anyone.','Yes, you needn’t to.'])
];
const listening=[
 A('choice','What was the aim of Nora’s experiment?','To practise being open through small conversations.','She did not aim to impress strangers or turn every exchange into a long conversation.','The goal was only to practise being open.','Use her explicitly stated goal, rather than assuming the experiment required confidence or impressive stories first.',['To practise being open through small conversations.','To impress every stranger with a long speech.','To stop enjoying quiet time permanently.']),
 A('choice','What had she usually done around strangers?','Looked at her phone instead of starting a conversation.','Using her phone felt safer and easier than initiating contact with unfamiliar people.','I preferred to look at my phone.','Compare her earlier routine with the deliberate experiment. The question asks about the period before it began.',['Looked at her phone instead of starting a conversation.','Started a deep conversation with everyone.','Asked every stranger to join her company.']),
 A('gap','How often did Nora plan to say something friendly to a stranger? Complete: once a ___.','day','Her simple rule was one friendly opening per day, without requiring a long exchange.','once a day, I would say something friendly to a stranger.','The question asks for the planned frequency, not how long each conversation had to last.'),
 A('choice','Why did the older man keep returning to the park?','It helped him feel close to his late wife.','He associated the park with his wife and continued visiting after her death.','it made him feel close to her.','Listen to the reason behind his ten-year routine, rather than assuming the birds were his only motivation.',['It helped him feel close to his late wife.','He was selling travel guides there.','Nora had asked him to wait on that bench.']),
 A('choice','How did Nora respond to his story?','She mostly listened.','Not knowing what to say did not prevent connection; listening was a meaningful response.','I did not know what to say, so I mostly listened.','Look for what she actually did, rather than assuming a successful exchange needs clever advice.',['She mostly listened.','She gave a long speech about productivity.','She immediately changed the subject to her phone.']),
 A('choice','How did she view brief replies from some people?','They were acceptable too.','The experiment did not demand that everyone continue talking or have a deep exchange.','That was fine too.','Connect this short conclusion to the different lengths of conversation described immediately before it.',['They were acceptable too.','They proved that the whole experiment failed.','They meant she should force a longer conversation.']),
 A('sequence','Put Nora’s experience in order.',['She notices that remote-working days feel disconnected.','She decides on one friendly opening each day.','She asks the older man about the park.','She grows more willing to speak when an opportunity feels natural.'],'Feeling disconnected motivates the rule, followed by the first conversation and later greater openness.','After that, I became braver.','Follow the sequence from the problem that motivated the experiment to the changed approach she keeps afterwards.'),
 A('choice','What limit does Nora keep at the end?','She does not force conversations.','She remains comfortable with quiet time and speaks when there is a natural opportunity.','I do not force conversations.','Look for the final qualification: greater openness does not become a duty to talk constantly or ignore others’ wishes.',['She does not force conversations.','She requires every exchange to last an hour.','She never allows herself quiet time again.'])
];
const vocab=[V('disconnected','feeling separated from other people','Nora can exchange many online messages and still feel this way. The word describes her social feeling, not only an internet fault.'),V('compliment','a comment expressing admiration or praise','A friendly remark about someone’s dog is an example. This is a positive comment, rather than a complaint or a request.'),V('queue','a line of people waiting their turn','Nora mentions waiting in one before the experiment. Think of people waiting for service, not a list of tasks in an app.'),V('brave','willing to act despite fear or discomfort','Nora becomes more willing to start conversations. This describes facing discomfort, not the absence of every nervous feeling.'),V('ordinary','normal rather than unusual or exceptional','A small question can change this kind of day. The word describes everyday experience rather than a particularly dramatic event.'),V('connection','a feeling of contact or shared understanding','The man thanks Nora for asking because the exchange creates this. It concerns a human relationship rather than train travel.')];

'use strict';

const cards=[
 C('Express a general preference.','I prefer tea to coffee.\nShe prefers walking to driving.\n\nPrefer + noun/-ing can compare general tastes with to.  C('Make a specific choice with rather.','I’d rather stay in than go out.\nI’d rather not drive.\nWould you rather walk or take the bus?\n\nWould rather + base verb; no to. Would sooner uses the same pattern and is less common.','Use than to compare the actions after would rather. Keep the forms parallel: walk than drive, not walk than driving.'),
 C('Use would prefer with an infinitive.','I’d prefer to leave early.\nI’d prefer not to drive.\nWe’d prefer to walk rather than take a taxi.\n\nWould prefer takes to + base verb; would rather takes the base verb directly.','Both are natural choices. Would prefer can sound a little more formal or polite in a particular request.'),
 C('Express a preference about someone else now.','I’d rather you didn’t call late.\nI’d rather we went by train.\n\nWould rather + subject + past simple expresses a present or future preference about that person’s action.','The past form softens or distances the preference; it does not place the call or journey in the finished past.'),
 C('Express a preference about a past action.','I’d rather you had called first.\nThey’d rather we hadn’t shared the photo.\n\nPast perfect after the second subject refers to a completed past action the speaker wanted to be different.','Compare didn’t call late for now/later with hadn’t called for the past.  C('Make a polite request with prefer.','I’d prefer you to email me.\nI’d prefer it if you didn’t call late.\n\nWould prefer + object + to-infinitive\nWould prefer (it) if + past simple','These express preferences and may still sound firm.  C('Keep comparisons natural.','I prefer reading to watching TV.\nI’d rather read than watch TV.\nI’d prefer to read rather than watch TV.\n\nThe to after prefer + -ing is a preposition.  C('Choose a realistic change.','Alexa finds that a clear instruction can still be hard to follow.\n\nI’d rather begin with ten minutes than change everything.\nI’d prefer you to suggest one manageable step.','Listen to the reason behind her old habit and the smaller replacement she chooses. Then negotiate a realistic routine in your own words.')
];

 G('choice','Which sentence compares general preferences naturally?','I prefer walking to driving.','Prefer + -ing takes to as a preposition before the second activity, with parallel -ing forms.','Look for the same grammatical shape on both sides of the comparison in the general preference pattern.',['I prefer walking to driving.','I prefer walking than drive.','I prefer to walking to drive.']),
 G('gap','I’d rather ___ at home tonight. Use stay.','stay','Would rather takes a bare infinitive, so stay follows directly without to or an -ing ending.','This is a specific preference using rather. Use the base verb rather than the to-infinitive used after would prefer.'),

 G('edit','Correct the pattern: I’d rather to leave early.','I’d rather leave early.','Would rather takes the bare infinitive leave, so the extra infinitive marker to must be removed.','The preference frame is already correct. Change only the form of the following infinitive group.'),

 G('gap','I’d prefer ___ leave at seven.  G('order','Build a polite preference about another person’s action.','I’d prefer you to email me.','Would prefer can take an object followed by a to-infinitive to express a preference about that person’s action.','Keep you after prefer and to before the action email.  G('rewrite','Use would prefer: I’d rather leave early.','I’d prefer to leave early.|I would prefer to leave early.','Changing from would rather to would prefer requires a to-infinitive while keeping the specific choice.','Keep the intended departure time. 'use strict';
const {C,G,A,V}=require('./lesson-authoring.cjs');
const cards=[
 C('Learn the pattern with the verb.','We decided to change the process.\nWe avoided copying the figures again.\n\nSome verbs take to + base verb; others take -ing.  C('Use -ing after a preposition.','Thanks for checking.\nShe is interested in learning.\nWe look forward to meeting you.\n\nA preposition is followed by a noun or an -ing form, not a to-infinitive.','The to in look forward to is a preposition. It differs from the infinitive marker in want to learn.'),
 C('Use an infinitive for an aim or decision.','He called to explain the error. → purpose\nWe agreed to try again. → verb pattern\nIt is hard to concentrate. → adjective pattern\nShow me how to use it. → question word + infinitive','Notice what comes before the action.  C('Leave out to after modals and some object patterns.','You should check.\nThey made us wait.\nLet me explain.\nHelp me carry / to carry this.\n\nModal + base verb; make/let + object + base verb. Help allows both forms.','The passive of make restores to: We were made to wait. Do not transfer the active pattern unchanged.'),
 C('Use common -ing patterns.','We enjoy solving problems.\nShe suggested checking the file.\nWe spent an hour waiting.\nThey had difficulty finding it.\n\nAvoid, finish, keep, mind and practise also commonly take -ing.','Learn the whole expression.  C('A different form can change the meaning.','Remember to lock it. → remember the duty, then act\nI remember locking it. → recall the action\nTry restarting it. → test a method\nTry to restart it. → make an effort\nHe stopped to rest. ≠ He stopped working.','Ask whether an action is remembered, intended, continued or stopped.  C('Recognise other contrasts.','Go on talking. → continue the same activity\nGo on to explain. → do the next thing\nI meant to call. → intended\nThis job means travelling. → involves\n\nI saw her cross the road. presents a whole event; I saw her crossing presents it in progress.','Begin, start and continue often allow both forms with little change.  C('Explain a process in your own words.','Mark’s team spent an afternoon building a template. They decided to change a routine that invited mistakes.\n\nRevisit the recording to distinguish the original procedure, the error and the new process.','This is a second listening to the supplied workplace story, with new questions. Use its problem-solving context to explain your own plan, not to memorise a script.')
];

 G('choice','Choose the correct verb pattern for a decision.','We decided to simplify the report.','Decide normally takes a to-infinitive in this pattern, followed by the base verb simplify.','Focus on the verb decided.  G('gap','We avoided ___ the same figures twice. Use copy.','copying','Avoid takes an -ing form when followed directly by another verb describing the avoided activity.','The action follows avoided directly. Use the activity form and change the spelling of copy appropriately.'),

 G('edit','Correct the pattern: We look forward to meet you.','We look forward to meeting you.','To is a preposition in look forward to, so the following verb takes the -ing form meeting.','Check the whole expression look forward to.  G('choice','Which sentence means a remembered past action?','I remember checking the file.','Remember checking recalls a completed experience; remember to check refers to remembering a duty.','Decide whether the memory is of an action already performed or a reminder to perform it later.',['I remember checking the file.','I must remember to check the file.','Please remember to check the file.']),
 G('gap','Please remember ___ send the final version. Use to or for.','to','Remember to send means remembering the required action before doing it, rather than recalling a past action.','This is a reminder about an action still to be done. Choose the marker for the duty pattern after remember.'),
 G('choice','“Try restarting the app” suggests…','testing a possible method.','Try plus -ing proposes an experiment to see whether the activity solves the problem.','The restarting is presented as a possible solution.  G('order','Build the pattern after spend + time.','We spent an afternoon building the template.','Spend a period of time is followed by an -ing form describing how that time was used.','Keep the time phrase after spent, then name the activity using its -ing form rather than an infinitive.'),
 G('edit','Correct the active make pattern: They made us to wait.','They made us wait.','Active make + object takes the bare infinitive, so to is removed before wait.','The sentence is active and names the people made to act. Keep the object and use a base verb directly after it.'),
 G('gap','She suggested ___ the numbers again. Use check.','checking','Suggest can take an -ing form directly; suggest to check is not the normal pattern taught here.','The suggestion is followed directly by an action, with no new subject. Use the activity form after suggested.'),

 G('rewrite','Use the passive with made: They made us wait.','We were made to wait.','The passive of make restores to before the infinitive while the object us becomes the subject we.','Change the receiver into the subject and add a passive form. Unlike active made us wait, the passive needs to.'),
 G('order','Build an -ing clause after a preposition.','Thank you for checking the figures.','For is a preposition, so checking names the activity after it in the -ing form.','Keep the expression of thanks together, then add for and the activity. The object belongs after checking.'),
 G('gap','They had difficulty ___ the right file. Use find.','finding','Have difficulty takes an -ing form for the action that causes the difficulty, without an extra preposition.','Complete the whole expression had difficulty doing something. Use the -ing form of the supplied action verb.'),
 G('choice','Which sentence emphasises an event seen in progress?','I saw her crossing the road.','The object + -ing pattern presents the action as ongoing when it was perceived.','Look for the perception pattern that focuses on a moment during the action rather than presenting the whole event.',['I saw her crossing the road.','I saw her cross the road.','I saw her to cross the road.']),
 G('edit','Correct the modal pattern: We should to check it.','We should check it.','Should takes a bare infinitive, with no to between the modal and the following base verb.','The sentence already expresses advice correctly. Remove the unnecessary marker after the modal.'),
 G('rewrite','Use means + -ing: This job involves travelling.','This job means travelling.|This job means traveling.','Mean plus -ing expresses what a job involves, rather than what someone intends to do.','Preserve the idea of involvement rather than intention. Both British and American spelling of the activity are accepted.'),
 G('choice','Which statement about start is accurate?','Both “started raining” and “started to rain” can fit.','Start commonly allows an -ing form or a to-infinitive with little difference in this example.','Do not force a false choice when a verb allows both patterns naturally in the stated situation.',['Both “started raining” and “started to rain” can fit.','Only “started rain” is possible.','An -ing form can never follow start.'])
];

 A('choice','What still needed a person’s input after the change?','A short comment.','The figures were taken automatically from the source files, while people still added a comment.','each person only had to add a short comment.','Separate what the template automated from the small part of the report that remained a human contribution.',['A short comment.','Copying all figures from three files.','Rewriting every original spreadsheet.']),
 A('gap','The improved report took about ___ minutes.','20|twenty','The new template reduced the work from almost two hours to about twenty minutes.','now took about twenty minutes.','Use the final duration after the change, not the afternoon spent building the template.'),
 A('sequence','Order the problem-solving steps, not the reporting routine.',['Mark notices the sent report contains old figures.','The manager questions the manual process.','The team builds a template.','The team spends less time producing reports.'],'Discovery leads to questioning the process, changing it and then seeing a faster reporting routine.','our team spent one afternoon building a simple template.','Follow the response to the error. 'use strict';
const {C,G,A,V}=require('./lesson-authoring.cjs');
const cards=[
 C('Report the message and its function.','She said the figures were missing.\nShe admitted missing the figures.\nShe promised to check them.\n\nDifferent reporting verbs describe different actions: stating, admitting and promising are not interchangeable.','Choose a verb that reflects what the person actually communicated.  C('Use a to-infinitive for an offer or promise.','He offered to help.\nWe agreed to wait.\nShe refused to answer.\nThey promised to reply.\n\nThe reporting verb is followed by to + base verb; the same person normally performs both actions.','Offer to help is natural. Offer someone help is another pattern, but offer someone to help is not the pattern for offering your own help.'),
 C('Name the person before an instruction.','She advised me to rest.\nHe reminded us to bring ID.\nThey warned her not to share it.\n\nAdvise, remind, tell, ask and warn can take person + to-infinitive. Put not before to for a negative instruction.','Use recommend doing or recommend that someone do/should do something as dependable teaching patterns; do not assume every reporting verb follows tell.'),
 C('Use -ing after the appropriate verbs.','He admitted making a mistake.\nShe denied taking the file.\nThey suggested checking together.\n\nAfter a preposition, use -ing: apologise for arriving late; insist on checking; accuse someone of copying.','Keep the required person and preposition where needed. Accuse someone of doing differs from admit doing.'),
 C('Distinguish say, tell and ask.','She said that she was ready.\nShe said to me that she was ready.\nShe told me that she was ready.\nShe asked me to wait.\n\nTell normally needs a person in this reporting use; say can introduce a clause without one.','Tell the truth and tell a story are other patterns. Here the focus is reporting someone’s message to a person.'),
 C('Keep statement order in a reported question.','He asked where the room was.\nShe asked whether we needed help.\n\nNo question inversion inside the reported clause. The whole reporting statement normally ends with a full stop.','Backshift depends on time and context. This lesson practises reporting patterns rather than a rule that every present verb must become past.'),
 C('Emphasise an earlier action if useful.','She admitted sending the file.\nShe admitted having sent the file.\n\nHaving + past participle makes the earlier timing explicit. The simple -ing form can also describe a completed past action when context is clear.','Do not assume admitted sending refers only to the present. Choose the perfect gerund when the earlier completion needs emphasis.'),
 C('Keep a summary faithful.','Julia suggests focusing on behaviour and asking questions. A useful summary preserves that advice without claiming she ordered everyone to agree.\n\nRevisit the feedback recording for its advice, examples and qualifications.','A new set of questions checks who says what and how strongly. Later, reporting passives will offer another way to attribute information.')
];
const tasks=[
 G('choice','Which sentence reports an offer by the speaker to help?','She offered to help.','Offer followed by a to-infinitive reports that the subject is willing to perform the helpful action.','Check who will do the helping.  G('gap','He apologised ___ arriving late. Complete the preposition.','for','Apologise for takes a noun or an -ing form naming the action for which the person apologises.','Learn the preposition with apologise. The following activity form is already provided and should remain unchanged.'),
 G('order','Report a reminder with a person and an infinitive.','She reminded us to check the figures.','Remind + person + to-infinitive identifies the people expected to remember and perform the action.','Keep us after the reporting verb.  G('edit','Correct the pattern: He suggested to check the report.','He suggested checking the report.','Suggest takes an -ing form directly in this pattern, rather than a to-infinitive.','The sentence has no separate subject for a that-clause.  G('choice','Which report preserves a refusal?','He refused to answer.','Refused to answer reports unwillingness to respond, rather than a promise or an admission.','Choose both the appropriate reporting meaning and the infinitive pattern that follows this verb.',['He refused to answer.','He promised to answer.','He admitted answering.']),
 G('gap','They accused him ___ copying the file. Complete the preposition.','of','Accuse someone of doing something keeps the person and introduces the action with of plus -ing.','The person being accused is already named. Complete the preposition before the action rather than changing its form.'),
 G('choice','Which sentence has a natural tell pattern?','She told me that she was ready.','Tell takes the listener me before the reported clause in this use, unlike say without a listener.','Look for the listener directly after told.  G('order','Report a negative instruction.','They warned us not to share the code.','Warn + person + not to-infinitive reports a negative instruction, with not before to.','Keep the people receiving the warning after warned. Put the negative marker before the infinitive action.'),
 G('edit','Correct the embedded order: He asked where was the office.','He asked where the office was.','A reported question uses statement order inside the clause, placing the office before was.','The reporting statement is already formed. Reorder only the words inside the where-clause.'),
 G('gap','She admitted ___ a mistake.  G('choice','What does “admitted having sent it” make explicit?','The sending happened before the admission.','The perfect gerund highlights completion before the reporting action rather than a future duty.','Notice having followed by a participle.  G('rewrite','Use promised + to-infinitive: “I will reply,” she promised.','She promised to reply.','The same person makes the promise and is expected to reply, allowing the to-infinitive pattern.','Keep the person who promised as the subject. Report the promised action with an infinitive rather than a quoted clause.'),
 G('order','Report an insistence with the required preposition.','He insisted on checking the data.','Insist on is followed by a noun or an -ing form, so checking names the insisted-on activity.','Keep on after insisted. The action then takes -ing because it follows the preposition.'),
 G('gap','She denied ___ taken the file. Complete the perfect gerund.','having','Having taken is a perfect gerund that explicitly places the disputed action before the denial.','Taken is already a participle. Add the -ing auxiliary that makes the earlier-action form after denied.'),
 G('choice','Which is a useful standard pattern after recommend?','I recommend checking the figures.','Recommend doing is a dependable pattern for advising an action without an explicit person object.','Choose the direct -ing recommendation, rather than applying the object pattern of tell to every reporting verb.',['I recommend checking the figures.','I recommend to check the figures.','I recommend that checking the figures.']),
 G('edit','Correct the say pattern: She said me that she was busy.','She told me that she was busy.|She said to me that she was busy.','Tell me or say to me can name the listener; say me is not the ordinary reporting pattern.','You may replace the reporting verb or add the preposition required by say.  G('rewrite','Use apologised for: She said sorry because she had missed the call.','She apologised for missing the call.|She apologised for having missed the call.','Apologise for takes -ing; both the simple and perfect gerund can refer to the clearly earlier missed call.','Name the apology with its reporting verb and preposition.  G('choice','Which report keeps advice distinct from a command?','She suggested checking the figures together.','Suggested reports an offered course of action rather than imposing an order or claiming the check is complete.','Choose the reporting verb that preserves the advisory force rather than making the speaker sound more authoritative.',['She suggested checking the figures together.','She ordered everyone to agree with her.','She announced that all figures were already correct.'])
];

 A('choice','Which report best preserves Julia’s qualification about feedback?','She acknowledges that some feedback may be unfair.','Julia explicitly allows for unfair or incomplete comments rather than requiring automatic agreement.','Sometimes feedback is unfair or based on limited information.','Listen for the limitation she adds to her advice, rather than reporting the whole talk as an instruction to agree.',['She acknowledges that some feedback may be unfair.','She promises that every manager’s comment is accurate.','She orders listeners to reject every uncomfortable comment.']),
 A('choice','What is the careless-person example intended to replace?','A personality judgement with a specific work example.','The suggested wording names missing numbers and a check instead of attaching a negative label to the person.','Instead of saying, “You are careless,”','Compare the two ways of speaking in the example.  A('choice','What does Julia imply about merely sounding gentle?','It may fail to communicate the needed change.','Gentle wording is insufficient when its vagueness stops the employee understanding what to do differently.','The message sounds kind, but it is also vague.','Separate a kind tone from a clear actionable message.  A('choice','Which timing recommendation matches the talk?','A brief discussion reasonably soon after the event.','Julia contrasts a timely short conversation with feedback delayed so long that the event is hard to remember.','A short conversation soon after the event','Use the comparison Julia makes about timing, without interpreting soon as interrupting someone in the middle of stress.',['A brief discussion reasonably soon after the event.','A long discussion after everyone has forgotten the event.','A public confrontation at the most stressful moment.']),
 A('choice','How can the listener avoid confusing a message with identity?','Treat a comment about work separately from a judgement about the whole person.','The talk shows that an unclear report can be heard as a judgement about professional worth, creating defensiveness.','Even when the comment is about one piece of work, it can feel personal.','Connect the report example to the explanation of defensiveness.  A('sequence','Order the contrasts in the talk.',['A comment about work may feel like a personal judgement.','Gentle wording may be too vague to help.','Specific behaviour can be discussed honestly and respectfully.','A listener can learn while questioning whether feedback is fair.'],'Julia moves through identity, vagueness, useful giving and finally the skills needed to receive feedback.','Receiving feedback is also a skill.','Follow the argument as presented, rather than sorting the statements by how important you personally consider them.'),
 A('choice','Which summary overstates Julia’s position?','She says being open means every criticism must be accepted.','Julia recommends openness while explicitly noting that feedback can be unfair or based on incomplete information.','That does not mean every comment is correct.','This question asks for the overstatement. ];

const {C,G,A,V}=require('./lesson-authoring.cjs');
const cards=[
 C('Put the receiver or result first.','The airline returned the suitcase. → active\nThe suitcase was returned. → passive\n\nPassive: be in the required tense + past participle. The original object becomes the subject.','Use a passive when the result matters or the doer is unknown, obvious or less important. Keep active voice when naming the doer is clearer.'),
 C('Change be to keep the time reference.','Bags are scanned. → routine\nThe bag was scanned. → past event\nThe bag will be scanned. → future\nThe bag has been scanned. → link to now\n\nThe participle scanned stays the same; the auxiliary group changes.','A passive is not automatically past tense. Identify the original time and aspect before choosing the form of be.'),
 C('Show work in progress.','The road is being repaired.\nThe bag was being checked when I arrived.\n\nContinuous passive: be + being + past participle.
