 G('choice','Which phrase describes preparing a drink?','make a coffee','Make a coffee is a natural phrase for preparing one drink; the prompt fixes this meaning rather than another idiomatic use.','Focus on preparing the drink.  G('gap','Could you ___ me a favour? Use do or make.','do','Do someone a favour is the established phrase for helping someone through a useful action.','The person me is the beneficiary, and a favour is the helpful act. Choose the verb learned with this phrase.'),

 G('order','Build a routine activity with do.','I do the laundry on Saturdays.','Do the laundry describes carrying out the routine washing activity, with the time phrase placed naturally at the end.','Keep do with the routine noun phrase.  G('gap','Did you ___ the appointment yesterday? Use the base form of make.','make','The past auxiliary did is followed by the base verb make, even though the appointment was arranged yesterday.','Did already marks the past question. Do not add the past form to the main verb after it.'),
 G('choice','In “Do you make the calls?”, the first do is…','the auxiliary forming the question.','Do-support forms the present-simple question while make remains the main verb of the calls collocation.','Identify the first verb’s grammatical job.  G('rewrite','Add emphatic did: I made a mistake.','I did make a mistake.','Emphatic did is followed by the base verb make, preserving the past event while stressing its truth.','Insert the past auxiliary for emphasis and return the main verb to its base form. Keep the noun phrase unchanged.'),
 G('order','Build an active causative with make.','The reminder made me stop working.','Made + object + base verb uses stop after me, followed by the -ing activity being stopped.','Keep me as the person affected, then a base verb after made. Working belongs with stop, not directly with made.'),
 G('gap','We were made ___ wait. Complete the passive causative.','to','The passive of causative make takes a to-infinitive, unlike active made us wait.','Were made already gives the passive. Supply the marker required before the action in this passive pattern.'),
 G('choice','Which phrase naturally describes completing a study activity?','do an exercise','Do an exercise refers to completing it, whereas making an exercise can mean creating the task itself.','The question fixes the learner’s role as completing an existing activity.  G('edit','Correct the collocation: We need to make research before deciding.','We need to do research before deciding.','Do research is the established collocation for carrying out an investigation; research is uncountable in this use.','The sentence concerns performing an investigation.  G('rewrite','Give a short affirmative answer: Does she make the calls?','Yes, she does.','The short answer uses does to match the present-simple question, rather than repeating make without its object.','Match the auxiliary and the singular subject.  G('choice','Which statement is a useful learning strategy?','Use the meaning guide, then learn the complete collocation.','The activity/result distinction is helpful, but established word partnerships and context still determine many choices.','Avoid assuming a simple meaning test predicts every phrase. Choose the strategy that keeps conventional usage in view.',['Use the meaning guide, then learn the complete collocation.','Use make before every noun naming any result without exceptions.','Use do only when the sentence has no other verb.'])
];

 A('choice','What made the initial system feel organised?','Detailed lists, deadlines, categories and priority levels.','Nathan invested effort in structuring his tasks, which created an organised feeling before its practical cost became clear.','divided them into categories, chose deadlines, and gave each task a priority level.','Look for what he did inside the system at the start. ];

'use strict';
const {C,G,A,V}=require('./lesson-authoring.cjs');
const cards=[
 C('Express one intended negative meaning clearly.','I don’t know anything.\nI know nothing.\n\nFor this ordinary meaning in standard English, use a negative verb with an any-word or an affirmative verb with a no-word.','Some English varieties use negative concord, where multiple negatives express one negative meaning. Recognising that pattern does not make those speakers less capable.'),
 C('Repair the pattern while keeping the meaning.','She didn’t go anywhere.\nShe went nowhere.\nWe don’t have any time.\nWe have no time.\n\nDo not combine don’t with no to express the same ordinary absence in standard writing.','Changing word forms can change scope or emphasis. First establish what is absent and keep the intended time reference.'),
 C('Treat hardly, barely and scarcely as negative-like.','I can hardly hear.\nThey could barely move.\nShe scarcely ever visits.\n\nThese already limit an action to almost none. Do not add an ordinary negative auxiliary for the same intended meaning.','Can hardly hear means hearing is very limited. It is not the same as hearing nothing in every situation.'),
 C('Use negative subjects with an affirmative verb form.','Nobody has arrived.\nNothing was missing.\nNeither option is suitable.\n\nThe subject carries the negative meaning; the verb normally has no extra not for the same meaning.','Nobody/no one normally takes singular agreement. Gender-neutral they/them can refer back to the person: Nobody called; perhaps they were busy.'),
 C('Match the scope you intend.','Not everyone agreed. → less than everybody\nNobody agreed. → no person\nI don’t think it is useful. → a negative judgement\n\nChoose negative placement carefully rather than treating all negative-looking sentences as interchangeable.','Separate clauses can each have a negative meaning: I didn’t leave because I wasn’t ready. Two negatives in different clauses are not automatically an error.'),
 C('Recognise legitimate combinations.','It is not impossible. → possible, often cautiously\nI can’t not help. → I feel unable to refuse to help\nIt was not without difficulty. → it involved difficulty\n\nSome combinations deliberately create a different meaning.','The simple one-negative guide is for avoiding unintended negative concord in standard usage. It is not a ban on every sentence containing two negative elements.'),
 C('Express a change over time.','He no longer works here.\nHe doesn’t work here any more.\nI haven’t finished yet.\nI don’t like it either.\n\nUse no longer with an affirmative verb, or not…any more, for something that has stopped.','For an ordinary negative agreement or unfinished action, use either or yet in the right position rather than adding another no-word.'),
 C('State a problem without overstating it.','Emma argues that cities need balance: quiet places need not remove all activity. Revisit her talk with new questions about what she rejects, allows and values.','In your own proposal, distinguish not all from none and almost none from zero. Keep your criticism clear without turning a limited problem into an absolute claim.')
];
const tasks=[
 G('choice','Choose the ordinary standard negative meaning “I know no facts about it”.','I don’t know anything about it.','A negative verb with anything expresses the intended absence without unintended negative concord in standard English.','Choose the standard pattern for the stated single negative meaning, not a dialectal pattern or a different logical meaning.',['I don’t know anything about it.','I don’t know nothing about it.','I know anything about it.']),
 G('gap','Nobody ___ arrived. Use has or have in standard agreement.','has','Nobody normally takes a singular finite verb, so has is used in this present-perfect sentence.','The meaning refers to no person, but the grammar of nobody is singular. Match the auxiliary to that subject.'),
 G('order','Build a standard negative with an any-word.','We don’t have any quiet space.','The negative auxiliary don’t combines with any before the noun phrase naming what is absent.','Keep the single ordinary negative in the auxiliary and use the compatible determiner before the noun phrase.'),
 G('edit','Keep the intended ordinary negative meaning: She didn’t go nowhere.','She didn’t go anywhere.|She went nowhere.','Use a negative verb with anywhere or an affirmative verb with nowhere to retain the intended standard-English meaning.','There are two valid repairs. Preserve the past event and absence of a destination while removing unintended negative concord.'),
 G('choice','Which sentence means hearing is very limited?','I can hardly hear.','Hardly already expresses an almost-negative amount, so can hardly hear means the ability is very limited.','Choose the natural standard pattern for a small remaining ability rather than adding another ordinary negative.',['I can hardly hear.','I can’t hardly hear.','I can hear everything clearly.']),
 G('gap','I don’t like the noise ___. Use either or neither at the end.','either','Either at the end of a negative clause expresses also not, without a second negative subject or inversion.','The negative clause is already formed. Complete the sentence-final agreement pattern rather than starting a new neither-clause.'),
 G('choice','What does “Not everyone agreed” establish?','At least one person did not agree.','Not everyone rules out universal agreement without establishing that nobody agreed.','Check the scope of the negative. It denies all agreeing, while leaving the number who did agree open.',['At least one person did not agree.','No person agreed in every possible case.','Every person agreed without exception.']),
 G('order','Build a negative subject with an affirmative verb form.','Nothing was missing from the room.','Nothing carries the negative meaning, and was missing describes the state without a redundant not.','Keep nothing as the complete subject. Do not insert an additional negative for the same intended meaning.'),
 G('edit','Correct the standard agreement: No one have called.','No one has called.','No one normally takes singular agreement, so the present-perfect auxiliary becomes has.','The negative subject is already suitable. Correct the auxiliary’s agreement rather than adding another negative.'),
 G('gap','He doesn’t work here any ___.  G('choice','Which sentence legitimately has two negative clauses?','I didn’t leave because I wasn’t ready.','The negative leaving and negative readiness are in separate clauses, each making its own contribution to the meaning.','Do not count negative words without considering clause structure. The two clauses here describe different states or actions.',['I didn’t leave because I wasn’t ready.','I didn’t go nowhere for the ordinary meaning I went nowhere.','Nobody didn’t arrive for the ordinary meaning no one arrived.']),
 G('rewrite','Use no longer: He doesn’t work here any more.','He no longer works here.','No longer supplies the negative meaning of discontinued work, with the affirmative third-person verb works.','Move the change-of-state meaning into no longer and remove doesn’t. Restore agreement on the main verb.'),
 G('order','Build a cautious positive possibility through understatement.','It is not impossible to improve this.','Not impossible allows the possibility of improvement, often with a cautious or understated tone.','Keep not with the negative adjective to create the intended cautious meaning. This is not ordinary negative concord.'),
 G('gap','We could ___ move in the crowded carriage. Use barely for very limited movement.','barely','Barely already limits the movement to almost none, so it does not need an extra negative auxiliary here.','The prompt asks for a very small amount of movement. Use the negative-like adverb without changing could.'),
 G('choice','What does “I can’t not help” usually express?','I feel unable to refuse to help.','The second not negates helping, and can’t rejects that possibility, producing a deliberate different meaning.','Interpret the scope of the two negatives rather than automatically rewriting the sentence as I cannot help.',['I feel unable to refuse to help.','I am completely unable to provide any help.','The phrase always means exactly the same as I can’t help.']),
 G('edit','Keep the standard absence meaning: We don’t need no extra noise.','We don’t need any extra noise.|We need no extra noise.','Use not with any or no with an affirmative verb for the ordinary absence of a need.','Preserve what is not needed. Choose one of the two standard patterns rather than keeping both negatives for the same meaning.'),
 G('rewrite','Use a negative verb and anything: I noticed nothing unusual.','I didn’t notice anything unusual.|I did not notice anything unusual.','The past negative auxiliary combines with the base verb notice and anything, preserving the original absence meaning.','Move the negative meaning from nothing into the verb phrase, and return noticed to its base form after did.'),
 G('choice','Which statement about negative concord is accurate?','Some varieties use it systematically; standard writing uses different patterns.','Negative concord is a grammatical pattern in some varieties, while learners can choose standard forms for contexts requiring them.','Distinguish an established dialect pattern from the conventions of the standard writing practised in this lesson.',['Some varieties use it systematically; standard writing uses different patterns.','It proves that speakers cannot reason about negative meanings.','Every combination of two negative elements is impossible in standard English.'])
];

 A('choice','What does Emma’s opening attitude make clear?','She enjoys city life while identifying a missing need.','Her positive examples precede the argument for quiet places, so the talk is not a rejection of cities as a whole.','most of the time I enjoy it.','Keep the positive opening and later criticism together. A specific need can be discussed without denying every benefit.',['She enjoys city life while identifying a missing need.','She wants all city businesses and buses removed.','She says there is nothing she likes about her city.']),
 A('choice','What does she reject about the definition of a quiet place?','That it must be completely silent.','Emma allows places with calm ordinary sounds, focusing on the opportunity to slow down rather than absolute silence.','A quiet place does not have to be completely silent.','Pay attention to what does not have to means.  A('gap','People should be able to sit without ___ anything.  A('choice','Why does she mention several groups of residents?','To show quiet places serve varied everyday needs.','Parents, older people, students and workers are examples of different people who can benefit from places to pause.','A quiet place can help many different people','Connect the list of groups to the claim about broad usefulness.  A('choice','What social change can places to pause encourage?','People notice their surroundings and each other more.','Emma contrasts moving quickly through roads and shops with observing neighbours, children and people resting.','people notice each other more.','Look for the social effect of pausing, rather than treating the argument only as a demand for zero sound.',['People notice their surroundings and each other more.','Everyone must start a conversation with every stranger.','Transport and shops become unnecessary in every neighbourhood.']),
 A('choice','Which limitation does Emma explicitly acknowledge?','Cities cannot remove all noise.','The talk accepts the need for transport, businesses and busy streets while asking for a better balance.','cities cannot remove all noise.','Preserve the stated limit of the proposal.  A('sequence','Order the argument about quiet spaces.',['City noise can create a continuing sense of alertness.','A quiet place gives people a chance to slow down.','Different residents benefit from accessible places to rest.','City design should balance activity with places to pause.'],'The talk moves from the pressure of noise to practical spaces, broad benefits and a balanced design conclusion.','good city design should include balance.','Follow the development of the argument rather than sorting the examples into an imagined city-building schedule.'),
 A('choice','What does the closing “not a small thing” communicate?','A little restored energy is treated as significant.','The negative understatement gives importance to the benefit rather than dismissing it as trivial.','And in a noisy world, that is not a small thing.','Interpret the final understatement in context. ];

'use strict';
const {C,G,A,V}=require('./lesson-authoring.cjs');
const cards=[
 C('Start with meaning and a timeline.','Ask: When? Is it a habit, event, process or result? What happened before what?\n\nTime words are clues, not automatic tense selectors. The same word can fit several forms when the intended meaning changes.','Choose the situation first, then build the form. In this review, connect present progress, past experience and future plans in one clear account.'),
 C('Contrast routine, temporary action and state.','I usually study at home. → present simple\nI’m studying at the library this week. → temporary activity\nI know the route. → state\n\nPresent continuous: am/is/are + -ing. Stative meanings normally prefer simple forms.','Some verbs change meaning: I have a bike is possession; I’m having lunch is an activity. Avoid a blanket ban based only on the verb’s spelling.'),
 C('Connect the past to now.','I’ve completed three tasks. → result/count\nI’ve been working all morning. → activity/duration\nI’ve known her since school. → state/duration\n\nSimple: have/has + participle. Continuous: have/has been + -ing.','For introduces a period; since a starting point. Simple perfect can also describe continuing states. Neither form alone tells you exactly how many cookies remain.'),
 C('Tell a past story and step further back.','We arrived late. → main event\nIt was raining when we arrived. → background\nI had booked the wrong date. → earlier event\nWe had been travelling all day. → earlier activity\n\nUse past perfect to establish earlier time; return to past simple when the order is clear.','A dated finished event normally uses past simple. Choose continuous forms for their process meaning, not because while or when mechanically requires them.'),
 C('Choose a future form for the intended job.','I’ll help you. → offer/decision now\nWe’re going to practise tonight. → intention\nI’m meeting Leo at six. → arrangement\nThe train leaves at seven. → timetable\n\nSeveral forms can be possible with different viewpoints.','Evidence can support going to predictions; will often gives opinions. These are useful contrasts, not a claim that only one future form ever fits a real situation.'),
 C('Locate future progress, completion or duration.','At nine, I’ll be travelling.\nBy nine, I’ll have arrived.\nBy June, I’ll have been working here for five years.\n\nWill be + -ing; will have + participle; will have been + -ing.','The last form highlights an activity’s duration up to a future point. With a state, use a simple perfect: we’ll have known each other for five years.'),
 C('Keep future time clauses in a present form.','When I arrive, I’ll call.\nOnce I’ve finished, we’ll leave.\nWhile you’re waiting, I’ll check.\n\nPresent perfect can highlight completion before the next action; present continuous can show overlap.','Compare an embedded question: I don’t know when she will arrive. That when-clause asks for information and is not a future time clause setting the main action’s time.'),
 C('Use the review in a real message.','Ethan’s story links preparation, setbacks and a changed routine. Revisit it with new timeline questions, then explain an experience, what you are doing now and a future plan.','Check whether your listener can follow the order and your purpose. Review one uncertain choice at a time, and use the course’s earlier topics for focused practice.')
];

Use own in the present simple for possession.','owns','The stative possession meaning uses present simple, with the third-person singular ending on owns.','The sentence describes possession rather than a temporary action.  G('order','Build a present-perfect continuous account of activity up to now.','I have been working on the project all morning.','Have been working highlights activity over the period leading up to now, rather than a specified completed total.','Keep have been before the -ing action.  G('edit','Correct the stative duration pattern: We have been knowing each other for years.','We have known each other for years.','Know normally has a stative meaning here, so present perfect simple expresses the continuing relationship.','Keep the connection from the past to now and the duration phrase, but use the simple perfect for the state.'),
 G('choice','Which form highlights a completed total up to now?','I have written three reports today.','Present perfect simple can emphasise the completed count of three reports in a period linked to now.','Focus on the specified completed number rather than the duration or effort of the writing activity.',['I have written three reports today.','I have been writing reports all morning.','I am writing a report now.']),
 G('gap','We have lived here ___ 2020. Use since or for.','since','Since introduces a starting point, while for would introduce a duration such as six years.','The number names the year the situation began, not a measured period of time.'),
 G('order','Build a past background interrupted by an event.','We were reading when the lights went out.','Past continuous sets the reading in progress; past simple introduces the event interrupting that background.','Keep were with reading for the ongoing scene and the simple past in the event clause after when.'),
 G('edit','Correct the earlier-past participle: I realised I had chose the wrong date.','I realised I had chosen the wrong date.','Past perfect uses had chosen to place the date selection before the later realisation.','The timeline is already suitable.  G('gap','They had been ___ for an hour before the bus arrived.  G('choice','Which sentence most directly offers help as a decision now?','I’ll carry that bag for you.','Will in this context naturally presents an offer made at the moment of speaking.','Use the purpose specified by the question.  G('gap','We’re going ___ practise tonight. Complete the intention pattern.','to','Be going to + base verb describes the stated intention, with to before practise.','Going is part of the future intention pattern here. Complete the group before the supplied base action verb.'),
 G('rewrite','Use present continuous for an arrangement: I have arranged to meet Leo at six.','I am meeting Leo at six.|I’m meeting Leo at six.','Present continuous can express a personal arrangement, with the meeting time retained in the sentence.','Keep the arranged future meeting and the person.  G('edit','Correct the future time clause: When I will get home, I’ll call you.','When I get home, I’ll call you.|When I get home, I will call you.','The ordinary when time clause uses present simple for future meaning, while the main clause retains will.','This when-clause sets the time for calling.  G('choice','Which sentence describes an activity in progress at a future moment?','At nine tomorrow, I’ll be travelling.','Future continuous locates the travelling as ongoing at the stated future time.','Distinguish what is happening at the moment from what has already been completed by that moment.',['At nine tomorrow, I’ll be travelling.','By nine tomorrow, I’ll have arrived.','I travelled yesterday at nine.']),
 G('gap','By Friday, we will have ___ the project. Use finish.','finished','Will have finished is future perfect simple, describing completion by the stated future deadline.','Will have is already supplied. Add the participle that expresses the finished result before or by Friday.'),
 G('rewrite','Use future perfect continuous: By June, my work here will have continued for five years. ];

const vocab=[V('setback','a problem that delays progress or makes a plan harder','The cancellation is one during Ethan’s trip.
